items.prompt: Why does looking at a distant galaxy always mean seeing it as it was long ago, rather than as it is right now?

options.label: Its light took a long time to cross the distance to us, so it left the galaxy well before it arrives here
options.feedback: Every bit of light reaching your eye set out on its journey however long ago the crossing takes, carrying a picture of the galaxy from that earlier moment, not from now.

options.label: Distant galaxies genuinely change more slowly than nearby ones
options.feedback: Nothing about a galaxy's own rate of change depends on how far away it happens to be from us; the delay comes entirely from how long its light takes to reach us.

options.label: Our eyes are naturally slower at processing very faint, distant light
options.feedback: Any delay in human perception is far too brief to explain a gap of that size; the true delay happened during light's long journey through space, long before it ever reached an eye.

options.label: Distant galaxies are somehow frozen in time compared with nearby ones
options.feedback: A distant galaxy keeps changing at its own pace just like any other; it only looks unchanged to us because we're seeing an old snapshot of it, not because it has actually stopped changing.

items.ok_line: The light you see set out long before it reached you.
items.ko_line: Nothing is frozen or slow out there — what takes the time is the crossing itself.
items.exp_text: Light carries a picture of whatever emitted it at the exact moment it left, and that picture stays unchanged for the entire time the light spends crossing space to reach an eye. Because that crossing can take an extremely long time across the distances between galaxies, the picture arriving now is one that was sealed up long before this very moment, showing the galaxy as it looked back then rather than as it looks today.

items.prompt: Why is looking farther out into space the same thing as looking further back in time?

options.label: Because a greater distance always means the light took a correspondingly longer time to travel here
options.feedback: Since light moves at a fixed speed, covering a bigger distance simply takes proportionally more time, so the farther out an object sits, the further back in time its light must have set out.

options.label: Because space becomes older the farther it is from Earth
options.feedback: No particular region of space is older or younger than any other simply because of where it sits relative to Earth; every part of the universe has been around for the same stretch of time.

options.label: Because light changes speed depending on how far it has to travel
options.feedback: Light's speed through open space stays the same over any distance; a longer journey means more time taken, not a different speed.

options.label: Because distant objects are somehow observed before their light even leaves them
options.feedback: Nothing can be seen before its light actually departs and completes the journey; what's being seen is always light that has already traveled the distance and arrived.

items.ok_line: More distance always means more travel time, so more time back.
items.ko_title: Distance and travel time go together
items.ko_line: At a fixed speed, a longer trip always takes longer — apply that directly to how old the light must be by the time it gets here.
items.exp_text: Because light travels at one fixed speed, the time its journey takes grows in direct step with how far it has to go, so an object twice as distant sends light that needs twice as long to arrive. Reading off an object's distance therefore also tells you how long ago its light departed, which is exactly why peering farther into space amounts to peering further back into the past.

items.prompt: Given how many stars and galaxies fill the universe, why is the night sky dark instead of glowing brightly with light from every direction?

options.label: The universe has only existed for a finite time, so light from the most distant regions hasn't had time to reach us and fill every gap yet
options.feedback: Filling the whole sky with light in every direction would require light from even the farthest reaches of an endless universe to have already arrived, and a universe with only a limited age simply hasn't allowed enough time for that to happen.

options.label: Stars are too small to be seen individually, so their light cancels out
options.feedback: Light from separate sources doesn't cancel itself out by arriving from different points; the darkness of the sky isn't a matter of light canceling, but of light not having arrived at all from the most distant regions.

options.label: Space itself absorbs and blocks nearly all starlight before it can reach Earth
options.feedback: Open space lets light travel through it essentially untouched over enormous distances; the darkness of the night sky isn't explained by space swallowing the light along the way.

options.label: There simply aren't enough stars in the universe to light up the whole sky
options.feedback: The universe holds an enormous number of stars and galaxies; a shortage of light sources isn't what keeps the sky dark — the limit is how much of that light has had time to reach us at all.

items.ok_line: Not enough time yet for the farthest light to arrive.
items.ko_line: The stars are there in huge numbers — ask instead whether their light has even had time to get here.
items.exp_title: A sky not yet filled in
items.exp_text: If the universe were endless in extent and had always existed, then in every single direction the line of sight would eventually run into some star or galaxy, and the whole sky ought to glow as brightly as a star's own surface. Because the universe has only existed for a limited length of time, light from the most distant reaches has simply not had the chance to reach us yet, leaving huge stretches of the sky between the visible stars still dark, unfilled by any light at all.

items.prompt: Why does the light from a very distant galaxy arrive stretched toward longer, redder wavelengths?

options.label: The space the light is traveling through is itself expanding, stretching the light's wave along with it during the journey
options.feedback: As the light crosses the growing distance between the galaxy and us, the very space carrying it is stretching, and that stretching lengthens the light's wave the same way stretching a coiled spring lengthens the gap between its coils.

options.label: The galaxy's light cools down like a fire dying out as it gets farther away
options.feedback: Light traveling through empty space doesn't cool the way a fire does; it can keep traveling essentially forever without losing energy that way — the shift toward red comes from the stretching of space itself, not from cooling.

options.label: Distant galaxies are made of different, redder-burning material than nearby ones
options.feedback: The galaxy's actual light doesn't need to be a different color to begin with for this to happen; the same light gets shifted toward red purely by the stretching it undergoes on its journey.

options.label: Dust between the galaxies filters out every color except red
options.feedback: Dust can dim and redden light somewhat when it happens to lie directly in the path, but the stretching seen in distant galaxies' light happens even along paths with essentially no dust, driven instead by the stretching of space itself.

items.ok_line: Space itself stretches the light on its way here.
items.ko_title: Think about the space in between
items.ko_line: Nothing about the galaxy's own light needs to change color at the source — ask what happens to the space the light crosses.
items.exp_text: As a beam of light makes its long crossing from a distant galaxy toward us, the space it is traveling through keeps expanding, and that expansion stretches the light's wave along with it, the way marks drawn on an inflating balloon spread farther apart as the balloon grows. A longer wave means redder light, so by the time it reaches an eye, the light of a very distant galaxy has been shifted noticeably toward the red end of its original color.

items.prompt: Why does light that has been stretched to a redder color, from a distant galaxy, point to that galaxy being both farther away and seen further in the past?

options.label: A longer journey through expanding space gives the light more time and more distance over which to be stretched, so more stretching means a longer, older journey
options.feedback: Space keeps expanding the whole time light is crossing it, so the longer that crossing takes, the more total stretching accumulates in the light's wave — heavily stretched light has therefore been on the move, and out of date, for a very long stretch of time.

options.label: Redder light always travels slower than other colors, causing it to arrive late
options.feedback: Light of every color travels at the very same fixed speed through open space; the reddening seen here isn't a difference in travel speed, it's a change to the light's own wave caused by the stretching of space during the journey.

options.label: The stretching happens instantly right as the light leaves its galaxy, unrelated to the length of the journey
options.feedback: If the stretching happened all at once at the moment of departure, it wouldn't tell you anything about how far or how long the light had since traveled — the whole point is that it accumulates steadily throughout the crossing.

options.label: Galaxies that are farther away happen to be built from intrinsically redder stars
options.feedback: A galaxy's true, close-up color doesn't depend on how far away it happens to be from us; the reddening being discussed here is added to the light during its journey, not present in the galaxy's light to begin with.

items.ok_line: More stretching adds up over a longer, older crossing.
items.ko_title: Think of it as building up over the trip
items.ko_line: The stretching isn't a one-time event at departure — it keeps accumulating throughout the whole journey.
items.exp_title: Stretching that adds up with distance
items.exp_text: Because the expansion of space keeps acting on light throughout its entire crossing, a beam that has been traveling for a very long time accumulates far more stretching than one that set out on a short hop nearby. Finding a galaxy's light shifted a long way toward red is therefore a sign that the light has been on its journey, and out of date, for an especially long stretch of time, meaning the galaxy sits especially far away and is being seen especially far back in the past.

items.prompt: What is the faint glow that fills the whole sky in every direction, older than the light from any galaxy?

options.label: Leftover light released when the early universe first cooled enough to let light travel freely
options.feedback: It is a remnant of the moment the young universe cooled past the point where light could finally escape and travel unobstructed, and that light has been stretched by the universe's expansion ever since, reaching us today as a faint glow from every direction.

options.label: Light reflected off the dust between every galaxy in the universe
options.feedback: This glow doesn't come from reflected light bouncing off scattered dust; it is light released directly by the hot, young universe itself, long before most galaxies had even formed.

options.label: The combined starlight of every galaxy that ever existed, blended together
options.feedback: This glow predates the very first galaxies and their stars altogether; it comes from an earlier stage of the universe, well before stars had formed at all.

options.label: Light given off by the space between galaxies as it slowly cools today
options.feedback: The glow isn't being freshly produced by anything happening today; it is old light that has been traveling since a specific much earlier moment in the universe's history, only now reaching us.

items.ok_line: A remnant flash from when the universe first turned transparent.
items.ko_line: This glow comes from before galaxies or stars existed at all — ask what changed in the universe itself to release it.
items.exp_text: In its earliest stage the universe was so hot and dense that light could never travel far before being scattered again, but as it expanded and cooled, it eventually reached a point where light could finally break free and travel onward without being stopped. That burst of newly freed light has been stretched fainter and redder by the universe's ongoing expansion ever since, and it now reaches us from every direction as a faint glow older than the light from any star or galaxy.

items.prompt: Why was the early universe too opaque for any light to travel through it, and what change finally let light move freely?

options.label: Free-roaming charged particles kept scattering every bit of light immediately, until cooling let those particles bind into atoms and stop blocking it
options.feedback: While loose, charged particles filled the young universe, any light trying to travel was scattered again and again almost at once; once cooling let those particles pair up into stable atoms, there was nothing left in the way to keep scattering the light, and it could finally travel freely.

options.label: The early universe was simply too dark, with no light being produced at all
options.feedback: Enormous amounts of light were being produced throughout the early universe; the trouble wasn't a lack of light, but that whatever light existed kept being scattered before it could travel any real distance.

options.label: Thick clouds of dust, exactly like the dust in a galaxy's disk today, blocked all the light
options.feedback: The barrier in the very early universe wasn't dust of the kind found in galaxies today; it was loose charged particles filling all of space at once, well before galaxies or their dust had even formed.

options.label: Light hadn't been invented yet as a physical phenomenon
options.feedback: Light already existed and was being produced throughout the early universe; the issue was that it couldn't get anywhere before being scattered, not that it didn't yet exist.

items.ok_line: Loose charged particles scattered light, until cooling let them pair up.
items.ko_title: Think about what was in light's way
items.ko_line: Light existed and was plentiful — ask what kept stopping it from getting anywhere.
items.exp_text: In its first stage, the universe was filled with loose charged particles that scattered any passing light almost as soon as it was emitted, the way a thick fog scatters a beam from a lamp before it can travel far. As the universe expanded and cooled, those charged particles slowed enough to pair up into stable, neutral atoms, and with nothing left to keep scattering it, light was finally free to travel onward across space without interruption.

items.prompt: Why does the very faintest, most stretched light reaching us from certain patches of sky count as evidence of some of the earliest galaxies that ever formed?

options.label: Such light has traveled, and been stretched by an expanding universe, for close to the entire age of the universe, meaning it left its source when the universe was extremely young
options.feedback: Light that has spent almost the whole history of the universe on its journey, accumulating that much stretching along the way, must have set out from its galaxy very close to the beginning of that history, when the universe itself was still extremely young.

options.label: Faint light always comes from small, unimportant galaxies rather than old ones
options.feedback: How faint a galaxy's light looks by the time it reaches us is governed mainly by how long and stretching a journey it has made, not by how large or important the galaxy itself was.

options.label: Stretched light is a sign that a galaxy is nearby but simply very dim to begin with
options.feedback: A nearby galaxy's light wouldn't have had nearly enough time or distance to accumulate that much stretching; heavy stretching specifically points to an especially long, and therefore especially old, journey.

options.label: The faintness shows that the galaxy has since been destroyed
options.feedback: How faint and stretched a galaxy's arriving light looks says nothing about what may or may not have happened to that galaxy since; it only reveals how long ago and how far away the light started its journey.

items.ok_line: A journey that long means a source that old.
items.ko_line: Faintness and heavy stretching together are markers of how long the light has been traveling, not of how big or how dim the galaxy truly is.
items.exp_title: A journey nearly as long as time itself
items.exp_text: The amount a beam of light has been stretched by the universe's expansion grows with how long it has spent crossing that expanding space, so the most heavily stretched light detected has been traveling for a span approaching the entire age of the universe. Light that old must have left its source when the universe itself had only just begun, which is exactly why such faint, deeply stretched light is treated as a glimpse of some of the earliest galaxies that ever formed.

items.prompt: Why can an event happening right now, in some far-off part of the universe, remain completely unknown to us for a very long time yet to come?

options.label: No signal of any kind can outrun light, so news of that event can only reach us after light has had time to cross the whole intervening distance
options.feedback: Whatever marks that event, whether it's light or any other signal, is bound by the same fixed speed limit that light obeys, so it still has to physically cross the entire distance separating that event from us before any trace of it can possibly arrive.

options.label: The universe deliberately hides distant events from view until they are ready
options.feedback: Nothing about the universe intentionally conceals events; the delay comes purely from the physical time light needs to cross a very large distance, with nothing acting as a deliberate screen.

options.label: Distant events only happen after a long delay, later than events happening nearby
options.feedback: An event far away happens at its own moment, on its own schedule; what's delayed is our knowledge of it, caused by how long its light takes to reach us, not the event's own timing.

options.label: Our instruments simply aren't sensitive enough yet to notice it
options.feedback: However sensitive any means of detection might become, nothing can shorten the physical time light needs to complete its crossing; the delay is set by the distance itself, not by how well anything can detect the light once it arrives.

items.ok_line: Nothing outruns light, so nothing outruns the wait.
items.ko_line: Whatever carries the news of that event still has to cross the whole distance first, at a fixed top speed.
items.exp_title: News that can never travel faster than light
items.exp_text: Any trace of a distant event, carried outward as light or as any other signal, is bound by the same fixed top speed, so it must physically cross the entire distance separating that event from Earth before it can possibly be noticed here. Across the vast distances between galaxies, that crossing alone can take an immense stretch of time, which is why something happening at this very moment, far off in the universe, can remain completely unknown here for ages yet to come.

items.prompt: Why might an object still visibly shining in tonight's sky no longer exist at all by now?

options.label: What's being seen is light that left long ago, and anything could have happened to the object in all the time since then, without any sign of it having reached us yet
options.feedback: The light arriving tonight is only ever a report from however long ago it set out on its journey, and whatever the object's true present state might be, news of any change since then simply hasn't had time to arrive.

options.label: Objects in the sky are permanent and essentially never actually change or end
options.feedback: Nothing in the sky lasts forever unchanged; every object has its own history and its own eventual end, quite apart from the separate fact that its light always shows an out-of-date view of it.

options.label: The light itself keeps the object alive for as long as it keeps shining toward us
options.feedback: Light traveling toward Earth has no influence at all on what continues to happen back at its source; the object's fate unfolds entirely independently of where its earlier light happens to be heading.

options.label: Only extremely faint, barely visible objects could possibly have already changed
options.feedback: This applies to bright and faint sources alike; regardless of how visible an object looks tonight, its light is still only ever a report from whenever that light actually departed, however long ago that was.

items.ok_line: You're seeing an old report, not a live view.
items.ko_line: What arrives tonight left a long time ago — ask what could have happened to the object in all the time since.
items.exp_title: A light with nothing to say about now
items.exp_text: Every bit of light reaching an eye tonight is a fixed record of its source at the exact moment it was emitted, and that record can never update itself or reveal anything about what has happened since. Because that emission could have occurred an extremely long time ago, whatever befell the object in all the years between then and now, including its own disappearance, could easily still be waiting, unannounced, somewhere out along the light's very long road to us.
